Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Acute onset (3 days) watery diarrhoea, mild central abdominal cramps, single vomiting episode, no blood, no fever.  
• Mild dehydration risk (low fluid intake).  
• Known asthma; currently stable.  
• Family history of colorectal cancer causing patient concern.

Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and DDx)  
1. Acute infectious gastroenteritis – likely viral (High likelihood).  
2. Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Moderate likelihood).  
3. Post-infectious/functional diarrhoea vs IBS (Low–Moderate likelihood).

Working diagnosis: Acute infectious gastroenteritis.

Management priorities  
• Prevent dehydration; monitor for red-flag features (fever, bloody stools, intractable vomiting).  
• Education on fluid replacement and rest.  
• Safety-net advice: attend in-person GP review if symptoms worsen, persist beyond a further day or two, or red-flags develop.  
• Reassurance regarding low likelihood of colorectal cancer given acute nature but acknowledge family history; advise routine screening with GP as appropriate.

Management Plan

- Advised to increase oral fluids (water, oral rehydration solution if available).  
- Avoid solid heavy meals; gradually reintroduce bland diet as tolerated.  
- No antibiotics recommended at this stage.  
- Stay home from work until symptoms improve to reduce spread and allow rest.  
- If develops fever, persistent vomiting, blood in stool/vomit, severe abdominal pain, or worsening symptoms, to seek urgent face-to-face medical review.  
- Follow-up: Patient to review with usual GP within 1–2 days if no improvement.  
- Provided reassurance regarding family history; suggested future discussion with GP about colorectal cancer screening.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Discuss at follow-up if anxiety persists – not actioned today.  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute infectious gastroenteritis – likely viral (High): classic sudden watery diarrhoea, cramps, brief vomiting, self-limited course.  
2. Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Moderate): similar symptom cluster; absence of fever/blood makes this slightly less likely than viral.
